specStatements.text: In solving quantitative problems, students should be able to recall and apply the following equations, using standard SI units.
Equations required for Higher Tier papers only are indicated by HT in the left hand column.
Equation 1: weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g) [symbol equation: W = m g]
Equation 2: work done = force × distance (along the line of action of the force) [symbol equation: W = F s]
Equation 3: force applied to a spring = spring constant × extension [symbol equation: F = k e]
Equation 4: moment of a force = force × distance (normal to direction of force) [symbol equation: M = F d]
Equation 5: pressure = (force normal to a surface)/(area of that surface) [symbol equation: p = F/A]
Equation 6: distance travelled = speed × time [symbol equation: s = v t]
Equation 7: acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken) [symbol equation: a = (∆v)/(t)]
Equation 8: resultant force = mass × acceleration [symbol equation: F = m a]
Equation 9: momentum = mass × velocity [symbol equation: p = m v]
Equation 10: kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)^2 [symbol equation: E_k = 1/2m v^2]
Equation 11: gravitational potential energy = mass × gravitational field strength (g) × height [symbol equation: E_p = m g h]
Equation 12: power = (energy transferred)/(time) [symbol equation: P = E/t]
Equation 13: power = (work done)/(time) [symbol equation: P = W/t]
Equation 14: efficiency = (useful output energy transfer)/(total input energy transfer)
Equation 15: efficiency = (useful power output)/(total power input)
Equation 16: wave speed = frequency × wavelength [symbol equation: v = f λ]
Equation 17: charge flow = current × time [symbol equation: Q = I t]
Equation 18: potential difference = current × resistance [symbol equation: V = I R]
Equation 19: power = potential difference × current [symbol equation: P = V I]
Equation 20: power = (current)^2 × resistance [symbol equation: P = I^2 R]
Equation 21: energy transferred = power × time [symbol equation: E = P t]
Equation 22: energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference [symbol equation: E = Q V]
Equation 23: density = (mass)/(volume) [symbol equation: ρ = m/V]
Students should be able to select and apply the following equations from the Physics equation sheet.
Equations required for Higher Tier papers only are indicated by HT in the left hand column.
Equation 1: pressure due to a column of liquid = height of column × density of liquid × gravitational field strength (g) [symbol equation: p = h ρ g]
Equation 2: (final velocity)^2 –(initial velocity)^2 = 2 × acceleration × distance [symbol equation: v^2 –u^2 = 2 a s]
Equation 3: force = (change in momentum)/(time taken) [symbol equation: F = (m ∆v)/(∆t)]
Equation 4: elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)^2 [symbol equation: E_e = 1/2 k e^2]
Equation 5: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change [symbol equation: ∆E = m c ∆θ]
Equation 6: period = (1)/(frequency)
Equation 7: magnification = (image height)/(object height)
Equation 8: force on a conductor (at right angles to a magnetic field) carrying a current = magnetic flux density × current × length [symbol equation: F = B I l]
Equation 9: thermal energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat [symbol equation: E = m L]

Equation 10: (potential difference across primary coil)/(potential difference across secondary coil) = (number of turns in primary coil)/(number of turns in secondary coil) [symbol equation: (V_p)/(V_s) = (n_p)/(n_s)]
Equation 11: potential difference across primary coil × current in primary coil = potential difference across secondary coil × current in secondary coil [symbol equation: V_p I_p = V_s I_s]
Equation 12: For gases: pressure × volume = constant [symbol equation: p V = constant]

scopeNotes.statement: Equations required for Higher Tier papers only are indicated by HT in the left hand column.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: In the recall list the only equation carrying the HT flag is momentum = mass × velocity (p = m v), so it is the only recall item here tagged tier 'higher'; its concept, its misconceptions and its question all carry that tier. Every other recall equation is tagged 'both', and no item tagged 'both' requires an HT-only equation.

scopeNotes.statement: Equations required for Higher Tier papers only are indicated by HT in the left hand column.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: On the equation sheet the HT flag falls on p = h ρ g, F = m ∆v/∆t, F = B I l, V_p/V_s = n_p/n_s and V_p I_p = V_s I_s. All items built on those five equations are tagged 'higher'; the remaining sheet equations are tagged 'both'. No Foundation-tier item asks for an HT-only equation.

concepts.term: Recall equation
concepts.definition: An equation in the first Appendix A list. It is not printed on any equation sheet, so it must be recalled from memory and then applied to solve quantitative problems. Recall means being able to write the equation, substitute values and rearrange it, not merely recognise it.

concepts.term: Standard SI units
concepts.definition: The unit set in which every quantity must be substituted: mass in kilograms (kg), length and distance in metres (m), time in seconds (s), force in newtons (N), energy and work in joules (J), power in watts (W), charge in coulombs (C), current in amperes (A), potential difference in volts (V) and resistance in ohms (Ω). Data given in grams, centimetres or minutes must be converted before substitution.

concepts.term: HT marking in the recall list
concepts.definition: Equations needed only for Higher Tier papers are indicated by HT in the left hand column. In the recall list the only equation carrying that flag is momentum = mass × velocity (p = m v); all the other recall equations are required at both tiers.

concepts.term: weight = mass × gravitational field strength (g), W = m g
concepts.definition: Recall equation 1. Weight W is in newtons (N), mass m in kilograms (kg) and gravitational field strength g in newtons per kilogram (N/kg). Mass is the same everywhere; weight changes when g changes, so the same object weighs less where g is smaller.

concepts.term: work done = force × distance, W = F s
concepts.definition: Recall equation 2. The distance s is measured along the line of action of the force, not simply the distance moved. Work done W is in joules (J), force F in newtons (N) and distance s in metres (m); one joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves an object one metre.

concepts.term: force applied to a spring = spring constant × extension, F = k e
concepts.definition: Recall equation 3. Force F is in newtons (N), spring constant k in newtons per metre (N/m) and extension e in metres (m). The extension is the increase in length from the unstretched length, not the stretched length itself.

concepts.term: moment of a force = force × distance, M = F d
concepts.definition: Recall equation 4. The distance d is the distance normal (perpendicular) to the direction of the force, measured from the pivot to the line of action. Moment M is in newton-metres (N m), force F in newtons (N) and distance d in metres (m).

concepts.term: pressure = force normal to a surface / area of that surface, p = F/A
concepts.definition: Recall equation 5. Only the component of force acting normal (at right angles) to the surface counts. Pressure p is in pascals (Pa), force F in newtons (N) and area A in square metres (m²); one pascal is one newton per square metre.

concepts.term: distance travelled = speed × time, s = v t
concepts.definition: Recall equation 6. Distance s is in metres (m), speed v in metres per second (m/s) and time t in seconds (s). Times quoted in minutes or hours must be converted to seconds first.

concepts.term: acceleration = change in velocity / time taken, a = ∆v/t
concepts.definition: Recall equation 7. The numerator is the CHANGE in velocity ∆v (final velocity minus initial velocity), not the final velocity. Acceleration a is in metres per second squared (m/s²), ∆v in metres per second (m/s) and time t in seconds (s).

concepts.term: resultant force = mass × acceleration, F = m a
concepts.definition: Recall equation 8. The force in this equation is the RESULTANT force - the single force with the same effect as all the forces acting. Resultant force F is in newtons (N), mass m in kilograms (kg) and acceleration a in metres per second squared (m/s²).

concepts.term: momentum = mass × velocity, p = m v
concepts.definition: Recall equation 9, Higher Tier only. Momentum p is in kilogram metres per second (kg m/s), mass m in kilograms (kg) and velocity v in metres per second (m/s). Momentum is a vector: it has a direction, taken from the direction of the velocity.

concepts.term: kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)², E_k = ½ m v²
concepts.definition: Recall equation 10. Only the speed is squared, and the whole product is halved. Kinetic energy E_k is in joules (J), mass m in kilograms (kg) and speed v in metres per second (m/s). Because the speed is squared, doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by four.

concepts.term: gravitational potential energy = mass × gravitational field strength (g) × height, E_p = m g h
concepts.definition: Recall equation 11. The height h is the VERTICAL height gained, not the distance travelled along a slope. E_p is in joules (J), mass m in kilograms (kg), g in newtons per kilogram (N/kg) and height h in metres (m).

concepts.term: power = energy transferred / time, P = E/t
concepts.definition: Recall equation 12. Power is the rate of transfer of energy, not an amount of energy. Power P is in watts (W), energy transferred E in joules (J) and time t in seconds (s); one watt is one joule per second.

concepts.term: power = work done / time, P = W/t
concepts.definition: Recall equation 13. Work done is one way energy is transferred, so this is the same rate calculation as P = E/t with work in place of energy. Power P is in watts (W), work done W in joules (J) and time t in seconds (s).

concepts.term: efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer
concepts.definition: Recall equation 14. The denominator is the TOTAL energy supplied, not the wasted energy. Efficiency is a ratio of two energies, so it has no unit; it may be given as a decimal or as a percentage, and it can never be greater than 1 (100%).

concepts.term: efficiency = useful power output / total power input
concepts.definition: Recall equation 15. The same ratio expressed with powers instead of energies, useful where a device is quoted in watts. Both powers are in watts (W); the efficiency itself has no unit and cannot exceed 1 (100%).

concepts.term: wave speed = frequency × wavelength, v = f λ
concepts.definition: Recall equation 16. Wave speed v is in metres per second (m/s), frequency f in hertz (Hz) and wavelength λ in metres (m). For waves of a given speed, frequency and wavelength are inversely related: a higher frequency goes with a shorter wavelength.

concepts.term: charge flow = current × time, Q = I t
concepts.definition: Recall equation 17. Charge flow Q is in coulombs (C), current I in amperes (A) and time t in seconds (s). Current is the rate of flow of charge, so charge and current are different quantities with different units.

concepts.term: potential difference = current × resistance, V = I R
concepts.definition: Recall equation 18. Potential difference V is in volts (V), current I in amperes (A) and resistance R in ohms (Ω). Rearranged it gives I = V/R and R = V/I.

concepts.term: power = potential difference × current, P = V I
concepts.definition: Recall equation 19. Power P is in watts (W), potential difference V in volts (V) and current I in amperes (A).

concepts.term: power = (current)² × resistance, P = I² R
concepts.definition: Recall equation 20. The CURRENT is squared, not the resistance. Power P is in watts (W), current I in amperes (A) and resistance R in ohms (Ω). Doubling the current in a fixed resistance quadruples the power.

concepts.term: energy transferred = power × time, E = P t
concepts.definition: Recall equation 21. Energy transferred E is in joules (J), power P in watts (W) and time t in seconds (s). To obtain an answer in joules the power must be in watts and the time in seconds.

concepts.term: energy transferred = charge flow × potential difference, E = Q V
concepts.definition: Recall equation 22. Energy transferred E is in joules (J), charge flow Q in coulombs (C) and potential difference V in volts (V). Potential difference is the energy transferred per coulomb of charge that passes.

concepts.term: density = mass / volume, ρ = m/V
concepts.definition: Recall equation 23. Density ρ is in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³), mass m in kilograms (kg) and volume V in cubic metres (m³). Density is a property of the material, so a large object and a small one made of the same material have the same density.

concepts.term: Physics equation sheet equation
concepts.definition: An equation in the second Appendix A list. It is printed on the Physics equation sheet, so it does not have to be memorised, but students must be able to SELECT the right one for the problem and apply it correctly - including rearranging it and substituting in standard SI units.

concepts.term: HT marking on the equation sheet
concepts.definition: Equations on the sheet that are required only for Higher Tier papers are indicated by HT in the left hand column. Those flagged HT are p = h ρ g, F = m ∆v/∆t, F = B I l, V_p/V_s = n_p/n_s and V_p I_p = V_s I_s; the remaining sheet equations are required at both tiers.

concepts.term: pressure due to a column of liquid = height of column × density of liquid × gravitational field strength (g), p = h ρ g
concepts.definition: Sheet equation 1, Higher Tier only. Pressure p is in pascals (Pa), height of column h in metres (m), density ρ in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³) and g in newtons per kilogram (N/kg). The pressure depends on the DEPTH below the surface, not on the total amount of liquid present.

concepts.term: (final velocity)² − (initial velocity)² = 2 × acceleration × distance, v² − u² = 2 a s
concepts.definition: Sheet equation 2. Final velocity v and initial velocity u are in metres per second (m/s), acceleration a in metres per second squared (m/s²) and distance s in metres (m). The equation gives v², so a square root is needed to obtain v.

concepts.term: force = change in momentum / time taken, F = m ∆v/∆t
concepts.definition: Sheet equation 3, Higher Tier only. Force F is in newtons (N), the change in momentum m ∆v in kilogram metres per second (kg m/s) and the time taken ∆t in seconds (s). For a given change in momentum, a longer time gives a SMALLER force.

concepts.term: elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)², E_e = ½ k e²
concepts.definition: Sheet equation 4. Elastic potential energy E_e is in joules (J), spring constant k in newtons per metre (N/m) and extension e in metres (m). The extension is squared and the product halved, which makes this a different calculation from F = k e.

concepts.term: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change, ∆E = m c ∆θ
concepts.definition: Sheet equation 5. Change in thermal energy ∆E is in joules (J), mass m in kilograms (kg), specific heat capacity c in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius (J/kg °C) and temperature CHANGE ∆θ in degrees Celsius (°C). The final temperature on its own is never substituted.

concepts.term: period = 1 / frequency
concepts.definition: Sheet equation 6. Period is the time in seconds (s) for one complete wave or cycle; frequency is in hertz (Hz), the number of cycles per second. Period and frequency are reciprocals, so a high frequency corresponds to a short period.

concepts.term: magnification = image height / object height
concepts.definition: Sheet equation 7. Both heights must be measured in the same unit, and because it is a ratio of two lengths the magnification has no unit. A magnification greater than 1 means the image is larger than the object.

concepts.term: force on a conductor (at right angles to a magnetic field) carrying a current = magnetic flux density × current × length, F = B I l
concepts.definition: Sheet equation 8, Higher Tier only. Force F is in newtons (N), magnetic flux density B in tesla (T), current I in amperes (A) and length l in metres (m). The equation applies when the conductor is at right angles to the magnetic field.

concepts.term: thermal energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat, E = m L
concepts.definition: Sheet equation 9. Thermal energy E is in joules (J), mass m in kilograms (kg) and specific latent heat L in joules per kilogram (J/kg). It is used for melting, freezing, boiling and condensing, where the temperature does not change, so no temperature term appears.

concepts.term: V_p/V_s = n_p/n_s
concepts.definition: Sheet equation 10, Higher Tier only. The ratio of the potential difference across the primary coil to that across the secondary coil equals the ratio of the number of turns in the primary coil to the number in the secondary. Both potential differences are in volts (V); numbers of turns have no unit.

concepts.term: V_p I_p = V_s I_s
concepts.definition: Sheet equation 11, Higher Tier only. For a transformer that is 100% efficient the power supplied to the primary coil equals the power delivered by the secondary. Potential differences are in volts (V) and currents in amperes (A), so a transformer that steps the potential difference up steps the current down.

concepts.term: For gases: pressure × volume = constant, p V = constant
concepts.definition: Sheet equation 12. For a fixed mass of gas held at constant temperature, the product of pressure and volume stays the same, so p₁V₁ = p₂V₂. Pressure and volume are inversely related: halving the volume doubles the pressure.

misconceptions.question: A mass is given as 250 g. What value is substituted into an equation?
misconceptions.correct: 0.25 kg - quantities must be converted to standard SI units before substitution.
misconceptions.misconception: Whatever number the question gives me is the number I put into the equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Substitution is treated as copying digits rather than handling quantities, and the unit is seen as a label attached afterwards rather than part of the value.
misconceptions.correction: Appendix A requires the equations to be applied using standard SI units. Convert first: grams to kilograms, centimetres to metres, minutes to seconds. Then the answer comes out in the SI unit too.

misconceptions.question: A time is given as 4.0 minutes. What is substituted for t?
misconceptions.correct: 240 s, because the SI unit of time is the second.
misconceptions.misconception: Time is time, so I can put 4.0 into the equation and write the answer in minutes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday timings are quoted in minutes and hours, and the equation symbol t hides the unit.
misconceptions.correction: Convert every time to seconds before substituting. Using 4.0 instead of 240 makes the answer 60 times too small, and answers in watts, joules or coulombs are only correct if the time was in seconds.

misconceptions.question: What does it mean that these equations must be recalled?
misconceptions.correct: They must be written from memory, rearranged and applied - they are not supplied in the exam.
misconceptions.misconception: I only have to recognise the equations; I will be given them if I need them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet the equation sheet in class and assume all equations are available somewhere in the paper.
misconceptions.correction: Only the second Appendix A list is printed on the Physics equation sheet. The first list must be recalled, and recall includes rearranging the equation and substituting SI values correctly.

misconceptions.question: A 12 kg rock is on Earth. What is its weight?
misconceptions.correct: About 118 N, found from W = m g with g = 9.8 N/kg.
misconceptions.misconception: Weight and mass are the same thing, so a 12 kg rock has a weight of 12.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech we 'weigh' things in kilograms, and bathroom scales are labelled in kg.
misconceptions.correction: Mass measures the quantity of matter in kilograms; weight is the force of gravity in newtons. They are linked by W = m g, so on Earth the weight in newtons is about ten times the mass in kilograms.

misconceptions.question: In which unit is weight given?
misconceptions.correct: Newtons (N), because weight is a force.
misconceptions.misconception: Weight is measured in kilograms, like the numbers on a set of scales.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Shop scales and food packets label mass in kilograms but call it weight.
misconceptions.correction: W = m g multiplies a mass in kg by a field strength in N/kg, and kg × N/kg leaves N. Any weight answer written in kilograms has the wrong unit and loses the mark.

misconceptions.question: An astronaut travels from Earth to the Moon. What changes?
misconceptions.correct: The weight decreases because g is smaller on the Moon; the mass is unchanged.
misconceptions.misconception: An object's weight is a fixed property of the object, so it is the same everywhere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: On Earth g barely varies, so weight looks like a permanent label attached to an object.
misconceptions.correction: In W = m g only m belongs to the object. Where g is smaller the weight is smaller, which is why a 60 kg astronaut weighs about 588 N on Earth but only about 96 N on the Moon.

misconceptions.question: A bag is carried horizontally by a vertical upward force. How much work does that force do?
misconceptions.correct: None, because there is no distance moved along the line of action of the upward force.
misconceptions.misconception: Any force moving with an object does work equal to force times the distance travelled.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is remembered as 'force times distance' and the bracketed condition in the specification is skipped.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states work done = force × distance (along the line of action of the force). Only movement along the direction of the force counts, so a vertical force and horizontal motion give zero work.

misconceptions.question: A spring 12 cm long is stretched to 20 cm. What is e?
misconceptions.correct: 0.08 m, the extension, which is the increase in length.
misconceptions.misconception: The e in F = k e is how long the spring is now.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The stretched length is the number the ruler shows, so it is the one students reach for.
misconceptions.correction: Extension = stretched length − original length. Using the total length gives a spring constant that is too small; here 4.0 N / 0.08 m = 50 N/m, not 4.0 N / 0.20 m = 20 N/m.

misconceptions.question: A force acts at an angle at the end of a 0.25 m spanner, 0.20 m from the pivot measured normal to the force. What is d?
misconceptions.correct: 0.20 m, the distance normal to the direction of the force.
misconceptions.misconception: d is just the length of the spanner or the distance to where I push.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In the usual classroom example the force is applied at right angles, so the lever length and the perpendicular distance happen to be equal.
misconceptions.correction: The specification defines d as the distance normal to the direction of the force. When the force is not at right angles to the lever, that perpendicular distance is smaller than the lever length.

misconceptions.question: A 600 N force acts normally over 0.30 m². What is the pressure?
misconceptions.correct: 2000 Pa, because pressure = force divided by area.
misconceptions.misconception: Pressure is force times area, so spreading a force over a bigger area increases the pressure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Multiplication feels like the default operation, and students recall 'force and area' without the division.
misconceptions.correction: p = F/A. A larger area over the same force gives LESS pressure - which is why wide skis stop you sinking into snow.

misconceptions.question: A pressure has been calculated from a force in newtons. What unit does the answer take?
misconceptions.correct: The pascal (Pa), the unit of the quantity being calculated.
misconceptions.misconception: The answer takes the unit of one of the numbers I substituted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students copy a unit from the question rather than deciding what quantity the answer is.
misconceptions.correction: Decide what the subject of the equation is and use its unit: pressure in Pa, power in W, charge in C, wave speed in m/s, period in s. The units of the substituted values do not carry through unchanged.

misconceptions.question: In an equation such as s = v t, does it matter which number divides which?
misconceptions.correct: Yes - the equation fixes the operation, and rearranging must follow the algebra.
misconceptions.misconception: If I am not sure, I divide the bigger number by the smaller one to get a sensible answer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Number-first thinking: students look for an operation that produces a tidy value instead of reading the equation.
misconceptions.correction: Write the equation, rearrange it symbolically, then substitute. 6.0 m/s for 240 s gives 6.0 × 240 = 1440 m; dividing would give 40, which is not a distance this cyclist could travel.

misconceptions.question: A car goes from 8.0 m/s to 20 m/s in 4.0 s. What is the acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: 3.0 m/s², from (20 − 8.0)/4.0 - the CHANGE in velocity divided by the time.
misconceptions.misconception: Acceleration is the velocity divided by the time, so I use the speed it ends up at.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol ∆ is read as decoration rather than as 'change in', and many textbook examples start from rest where the two happen to be equal.
misconceptions.correction: a = ∆v/t and ∆v = final velocity − initial velocity. Starting from rest the initial velocity is zero, which is the only case where using the final velocity alone happens to work.

misconceptions.question: A car has a 4000 N driving force and 1000 N of resistive forces. Which force goes into F = m a?
misconceptions.correct: The resultant force, 3000 N.
misconceptions.misconception: F = m a uses the force that is pushing the object - the engine's force.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The driving force is the one named in the question and feels like the cause of the motion.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states resultant force = mass × acceleration. Combine all the forces first: 4000 N − 1000 N = 3000 N, so a = 3000/1200 = 2.5 m/s².

misconceptions.question: How are a 4000 N driving force and 1000 N of resistive forces combined?
misconceptions.correct: They are subtracted, because they act in opposite directions, giving 3000 N.
misconceptions.misconception: To find the resultant you add all the forces acting on the object together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Resultant' is heard as 'total', and direction is dropped when only sizes are written down.
misconceptions.correction: Force is a vector. Forces in opposite directions subtract; only forces in the same direction add. Adding here would give 5000 N and an acceleration that is too large.

misconceptions.question: In which unit is momentum given?
misconceptions.correct: Kilogram metres per second (kg m/s).
misconceptions.misconception: Momentum is a kind of force, so it is measured in newtons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language treats momentum as a push, and the symbol p is also used for pressure.
misconceptions.correction: p = m v multiplies kg by m/s, so the unit is kg m/s. Force is a different quantity, related to momentum by F = m ∆v/∆t.

misconceptions.question: Does the velocity get squared when finding momentum?
misconceptions.correct: No - momentum = mass × velocity, with the velocity to the power one.
misconceptions.misconception: Momentum is like kinetic energy, so I square the velocity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both equations pair mass with velocity, and the squaring in ½ m v² is memorable enough to leak into p = m v.
misconceptions.correction: Only kinetic energy squares the speed. For a 0.45 kg ball at 12 m/s the momentum is 0.45 × 12 = 5.4 kg m/s, whereas the kinetic energy would be 0.5 × 0.45 × 12² = 32 J.

misconceptions.question: A 60 kg runner moves at 4.0 m/s. What is the kinetic energy?
misconceptions.misconception: Kinetic energy is half the mass times the speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The exponent is small in print and is lost when the equation is copied from memory under pressure.
misconceptions.correction: The specification writes kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)². Square the speed first: 4.0² = 16, then 0.5 × 60 × 16 = 480 J, not 120 J.

misconceptions.question: Where does the 0.5 go in the kinetic energy equation?
misconceptions.correct: It multiplies the whole product: E_k = 0.5 × m × v².
misconceptions.misconception: The equation is just mass times speed squared; the half is a detail I can leave out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The half looks like a small correction next to the squaring, so it is dropped when recall is shaky.
misconceptions.correction: Omitting the 0.5 doubles every answer: 60 × 16 = 960 J instead of 480 J. Both the half and the square are part of the recalled equation.

misconceptions.question: A car's speed doubles. What happens to its kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: It becomes four times as large, because the speed is squared.
misconceptions.misconception: If the speed doubles then the kinetic energy doubles too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat every relationship as directly proportional and read past the square.
misconceptions.correction: In E_k = 0.5 m v², doubling v multiplies v² by 2² = 4. This is why stopping distances grow so sharply with speed.

misconceptions.question: Does kinetic energy depend on speed as well as mass?
misconceptions.correct: Yes - it depends on the mass and on the square of the speed.
misconceptions.misconception: Kinetic energy is really about how heavy something is, so changing the speed hardly matters.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass is the quantity students can see and weigh, while speed feels like a temporary condition.
misconceptions.correction: Both appear in E_k = 0.5 m v², and the speed appears squared, so speed has the stronger effect. A change in speed with unchanged mass changes the kinetic energy.

misconceptions.question: A box is pushed 5.0 m up a ramp, rising 1.5 m vertically. Which is h?
misconceptions.correct: 1.5 m, the vertical height gained.
misconceptions.misconception: h is how far the object travelled up the slope.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The distance along the slope is the length that is drawn and measured, and 'height' is read as 'distance moved upwards along the path'.
misconceptions.correction: E_p = m g h uses vertical height only. Using 5.0 m instead of 1.5 m here would give 98 J instead of the correct 29 J.

misconceptions.question: Which three quantities are multiplied for gravitational potential energy?
misconceptions.correct: Mass, gravitational field strength and height.
misconceptions.misconception: Gravitational potential energy is just mass times height.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The g is easy to drop because its value looks like a constant that will 'sort itself out'.
misconceptions.correction: E_p = m g h. Leaving out g = 9.8 N/kg makes the answer about ten times too small - 3.0 J instead of 29 J.

misconceptions.question: What is the difference between power and energy transferred?
misconceptions.correct: Power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts; energy is measured in joules.
misconceptions.misconception: Power and energy are the same thing, so a big energy transfer means a big power.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language uses 'power' loosely for anything energetic, and both are met in the same lessons.
misconceptions.correction: P = E/t. The same 360 000 J transferred in 180 s gives 2000 W, but in 3600 s it gives only 100 W. The time taken is what makes the two different.

misconceptions.question: A device transfers 250 J usefully from an input of 1000 J. What is its efficiency?
misconceptions.correct: 0.25, from useful output divided by total input.
misconceptions.misconception: Efficiency is total input divided by useful output, so it can come out bigger than 1.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students divide the larger number by the smaller to avoid a decimal answer.
misconceptions.correction: The useful output is on top. Efficiency can never exceed 1 or 100%, so any answer above 1 shows the fraction has been inverted.

misconceptions.question: Which energy goes on the bottom of the efficiency equation?
misconceptions.correct: The total input energy transfer.
misconceptions.misconception: You compare the useful energy with the energy that was wasted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lessons emphasise wasted energy, so it becomes the memorable second quantity.
misconceptions.correction: efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer. With 250 J useful out of 1000 J in, the efficiency is 0.25, not 250/750.

misconceptions.question: What unit does efficiency have?
misconceptions.correct: None - it is a ratio of two energies, written as a decimal or a percentage.
misconceptions.misconception: Efficiency is an amount of energy, so I give the answer in joules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities in the fraction are energies, so students expect joules in the answer.
misconceptions.correction: Dividing joules by joules cancels the unit. Quoting an efficiency as '750 J' confuses the wasted energy with the efficiency itself.

misconceptions.question: A source on the same string is changed to a higher frequency. What happens to the wave speed?
misconceptions.correct: It stays the same; the wavelength becomes shorter instead.
misconceptions.misconception: Increasing the frequency must increase the wave speed, because v = f λ has f in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is read as a one-way rule, and the fact that λ changes at the same time is ignored.
misconceptions.correction: In a given medium the speed is fixed, so f and λ are inversely related: if f doubles, λ halves and the product f λ is unchanged.

misconceptions.question: How are charge flow and current different?
misconceptions.correct: Current is the rate of flow of charge; charge flow is current multiplied by the time.
misconceptions.misconception: Charge and current are two words for the same thing, so a 0.50 A current means 0.50 C.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are described as 'electricity flowing', and the difference only appears once time is involved.
misconceptions.correction: Q = I t. A current of 0.50 A for 240 s delivers 120 C. Charge is in coulombs, current in amperes.

misconceptions.question: A 12 Ω resistor carries 0.25 A. What is the potential difference?
misconceptions.correct: 3.0 V, from V = I R.
misconceptions.misconception: To find potential difference you divide the current by the resistance, or the resistance by the current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two of the three quantities are given and students pick an operation by feel rather than rearranging the equation.
misconceptions.correction: V = I R means multiply: 0.25 × 12 = 3.0 V. Only when V is known do you divide, as in I = V/R and R = V/I.

misconceptions.question: In P = I² R, which quantity is squared?
misconceptions.correct: The current.
misconceptions.misconception: You square the resistance, because R is the bigger number in the equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The superscript is attached to whichever symbol the student remembers as important, and R often carries the larger value.
misconceptions.correction: P = (current)² × resistance. For 3.0 A in 20 Ω the power is 3.0² × 20 = 180 W, not 3.0 × 20² = 1200 W.

misconceptions.question: Is P = I² R the same as multiplying current by resistance?
misconceptions.correct: No - the current must be squared first.
misconceptions.misconception: Power is just current times resistance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is confused with V = I R, which does simply multiply the two.
misconceptions.correction: I R gives a potential difference in volts, not a power. Squaring the current first gives 3.0² × 20 = 180 W, while 3.0 × 20 = 60 gives the wrong quantity as well as the wrong number.

misconceptions.question: A charge of 15 C passes through a potential difference of 12 V. What energy is transferred?
misconceptions.correct: 180 J, from E = Q V.
misconceptions.misconception: Potential difference is energy per coulomb, so I divide the charge by the potential difference.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The definition of the volt as 'joules per coulomb' is half-remembered and the division is applied the wrong way round.
misconceptions.correction: V = E/Q rearranges to E = Q V, so multiply: 15 × 12 = 180 J. Dividing gives 1.25, which is neither an energy nor a sensible size.

misconceptions.question: A block has a mass of 5.4 kg and a volume of 0.0020 m³. What is its density?
misconceptions.correct: 2700 kg/m³, from mass divided by volume.
misconceptions.misconception: Density is volume divided by mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is remembered as a pair of words without their order, and dividing by a small decimal produces an uncomfortably large number that students distrust.
misconceptions.correction: ρ = m/V puts mass on top: 5.4 / 0.0020 = 2700 kg/m³. The unit kg/m³ itself shows which quantity divides which.

misconceptions.question: Which equations are printed on the Physics equation sheet?
misconceptions.correct: Only those in the second Appendix A list; the first list must be recalled.
misconceptions.misconception: All the physics equations are on the equation sheet, so there is nothing to learn.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The sheet is present in every paper, so students assume it is complete.
misconceptions.correction: The sheet carries twelve equations. The twenty-three in the recall list, including W = m g, E_p = m g h and efficiency, are not on it and must be memorised.

misconceptions.question: How can you tell which equations are given on the sheet?
misconceptions.correct: By learning which list each equation is in - length is no guide.
misconceptions.misconception: The long, complicated-looking equations are given and only the short ones need learning.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students judge the effort of memorising by how the equation looks on the page.
misconceptions.correction: Some recall equations are long, such as gravitational potential energy = mass × gravitational field strength × height, while short ones such as period = 1/frequency are on the sheet.

misconceptions.question: Which three quantities are multiplied for the pressure due to a column of liquid?
misconceptions.correct: Height of the column, density of the liquid and gravitational field strength.
misconceptions.misconception: It is just the depth times the density of the liquid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two of the three quantities are named in the question stem, and g is treated as an optional constant.
misconceptions.correction: p = h ρ g. Leaving out g = 9.8 N/kg gives 3000 Pa instead of 29 400 Pa for 3.0 m of water.

misconceptions.question: Why is the pressure greater at the bottom of a deep tank than near the surface?
misconceptions.correct: Because the height of liquid above that point is greater, and p = h ρ g.
misconceptions.misconception: The pressure depends on how much liquid there is in total, not on how deep you are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A big tank obviously holds more liquid, so total quantity feels like the cause of the pressure.
misconceptions.correction: Only h, ρ and g appear in the equation. A narrow tube and a wide tank filled to the same depth with the same liquid give the same pressure at the bottom.

misconceptions.question: A car starts at 5.0 m/s and accelerates at 2.0 m/s² over 12 m. What is its final velocity?
misconceptions.correct: 8.5 m/s, after taking the square root of v².
misconceptions.misconception: The equation gives me v straight away, so the number I work out is the final velocity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The square symbol is attached to v at the start of the equation and forgotten by the end of the arithmetic.
misconceptions.correction: v² − u² = 2 a s gives v² = 5.0² + 2 × 2.0 × 12 = 73, so v = √73 = 8.5 m/s. Quoting 73 m/s gives a speed faster than a car on a motorway.

misconceptions.question: Can the initial velocity be left out if the object is already moving?
misconceptions.correct: No - u² must be included whenever the object has an initial velocity.
misconceptions.misconception: I can just use 2 a s to get v², because that is the side with the numbers in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most first examples start from rest, where u = 0 and the term genuinely disappears.
misconceptions.correction: Rearranged, v² = u² + 2 a s. Dropping u² here gives √48 = 6.9 m/s instead of 8.5 m/s.

misconceptions.question: A car is stopped in a longer time in a crash. What happens to the force on it?
misconceptions.correct: The force is smaller, because the same change in momentum is spread over a longer time.
misconceptions.misconception: A longer collision means a bigger force, so I multiply the momentum change by the time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Longer contact sounds more severe, and multiplying avoids dividing by an awkward decimal.
misconceptions.correction: F = m ∆v/∆t has ∆t on the bottom. Crumple zones and air bags work by increasing ∆t to reduce the force: 1200 × 15 / 0.20 = 90 000 N, but over 2.0 s it would be only 9000 N.

misconceptions.question: What must be done with the change in momentum to obtain the force?
misconceptions.correct: Divide it by the time taken for the change.
misconceptions.misconception: The force is just the mass multiplied by the change in velocity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The change in momentum m ∆v is calculated first and then reported as the answer before the division is done.
misconceptions.correction: The quantity m ∆v is a momentum change in kg m/s, not a force. Dividing by ∆t = 0.20 s converts 18 000 kg m/s into 90 000 N.

misconceptions.question: A spring with k = 200 N/m is extended by 0.30 m. What elastic potential energy is stored?
misconceptions.misconception: I work out the force from F = k e and give that as the energy stored.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both equations use k and e, so the more familiar F = k e is selected from the sheet by mistake.
misconceptions.correction: F = k e gives a force in newtons, here 60 N. Energy needs E_e = 0.5 k e² = 0.5 × 200 × 0.09 = 9.0 J.

misconceptions.question: Is the extension squared in the elastic potential energy equation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes - elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)².
misconceptions.misconception: I halve the spring constant and multiply by the extension once.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is copied from the sheet in a hurry and the small superscript on e is missed.
misconceptions.correction: Squaring matters: 0.5 × 200 × 0.30² = 9.0 J, whereas 0.5 × 200 × 0.30 = 30 J is three times too large.

misconceptions.question: Water is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. Which temperature goes into ∆E = m c ∆θ?
misconceptions.correct: The temperature CHANGE, 50 °C.
misconceptions.misconception: I substitute the temperature it reaches, because that is the temperature of the water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol θ is familiar as 'temperature' and the ∆ in front of it is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: ∆θ is the change: 70 − 20 = 50 °C. Using 70 would give 588 000 J instead of the correct 420 000 J.

misconceptions.question: How many quantities are multiplied in ∆E = m c ∆θ?
misconceptions.correct: Three: mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change.
misconceptions.misconception: Thermal energy is just the mass times the specific heat capacity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two quantities printed in the data are used and the temperature change, which has to be worked out, is left aside.
misconceptions.correction: All three factors are needed. Omitting ∆θ = 50 °C gives 8400 J rather than 420 000 J.

misconceptions.question: A wave has a frequency of 250 Hz. What is its period?
misconceptions.correct: 0.0040 s, because period = 1/frequency.
misconceptions.misconception: The period and the frequency are the same number, just written differently.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both describe the timing of a wave and are introduced together, so they merge in memory.
misconceptions.correction: They are reciprocals. A frequency of 250 Hz means 250 cycles each second, so one cycle takes 1/250 = 0.0040 s.

misconceptions.question: An object 4.0 mm tall produces an image 26 mm tall. What is the magnification?
misconceptions.correct: 6.5, from image height divided by object height.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnification is the object height divided by the image height.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The object is met first in the ray diagram, so it is written first in the fraction.
misconceptions.correction: magnification = image height / object height, so 26/4.0 = 6.5. An answer of 0.15 would mean the image was smaller than the object.

misconceptions.question: What unit does a magnification have?
misconceptions.correct: None - it is a ratio of two lengths measured in the same unit.
misconceptions.misconception: Magnification is measured in millimetres, because the heights were in millimetres.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry a unit through from the data instead of asking whether the units cancel.
misconceptions.correction: Dividing mm by mm cancels the unit, so a magnification is written as a plain number such as 6.5.

misconceptions.question: A 0.25 m conductor in a 0.40 T field carries 3.0 A at right angles. What is the force on it?
misconceptions.correct: 0.30 N, from F = B I l.
misconceptions.misconception: The force is just the flux density times the current.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The length is the least memorable of the three quantities and is easily left out of the product.
misconceptions.correction: All three are needed: 0.40 × 3.0 × 0.25 = 0.30 N. Omitting the length gives 1.2 N, four times too large.

misconceptions.question: Does F = B I l apply however the conductor lies in the field?
misconceptions.correct: No - the equation as given applies to a conductor at right angles to the magnetic field.
misconceptions.misconception: The equation works for any orientation of the wire in the field.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The condition sits in brackets in the equation's wording and is skipped when the symbols are copied.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states 'force on a conductor (at right angles to a magnetic field) carrying a current'. A conductor lying along the field direction experiences no force at all.

misconceptions.question: Ice of mass 0.50 kg melts. Which quantities are multiplied?
misconceptions.correct: The mass and the specific latent heat.
misconceptions.misconception: The specific latent heat is the energy needed to melt it, so that is the answer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'specific' is not read as 'per kilogram', so the tabulated value looks like a total.
misconceptions.correction: Specific latent heat is the energy per kilogram, so it must be multiplied by the mass: 0.50 × 340 000 = 170 000 J.

misconceptions.question: Which equation is used while ice is melting at 0 °C?
misconceptions.correct: E = m L, the equation for a change of state.
misconceptions.misconception: I use mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change, as for any heating.
misconceptions.whyItArises: ∆E = m c ∆θ is met first and is used for anything involving thermal energy.
misconceptions.correction: During a change of state the temperature does not change, so ∆θ would be zero. The energy goes into breaking the bonds between particles and is found from E = m L.

misconceptions.question: A transformer has 200 primary turns, 1000 secondary turns and 230 V across the primary. What is the secondary potential difference?
misconceptions.correct: 1150 V - more turns on the secondary means a larger potential difference.
misconceptions.misconception: I divide by the turns ratio, so more secondary turns must give a smaller potential difference.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The ratio is written with the primary on top on both sides, and students match the wrong pair when they cross-multiply.
misconceptions.correction: V_p/V_s = n_p/n_s gives 230/V_s = 200/1000, so V_s = 230 × 1000/200 = 1150 V. Getting 46 V means the ratio was used upside down.

misconceptions.question: A transformer steps the potential difference up. What happens to the current?
misconceptions.correct: It steps down, because V_p I_p = V_s I_s.
misconceptions.misconception: A step-up transformer increases the potential difference and the current, so you get more power out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Step-up' sounds like an all-round increase, and the link to conservation of energy is not made.
misconceptions.correction: The equation states that the power in equals the power out. If the potential difference rises five times, the current falls to a fifth: 230 × 2.0 = 1150 × 0.40.

misconceptions.question: Does the current stay the same on both sides of a transformer?
misconceptions.correct: No - only the product of potential difference and current is the same on each side.
misconceptions.misconception: The same current flows all the way round, so the current in both coils is equal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two coils are pictured as one circuit, and series circuit rules are applied to them.
misconceptions.correction: The coils are separate circuits linked by a magnetic field. V_p I_p = V_s I_s, so with 230 V and 2.0 A in, a 1150 V secondary carries only 0.40 A.

misconceptions.question: A gas at constant temperature is compressed to a smaller volume. What happens to the pressure?
misconceptions.correct: It increases, because pressure × volume stays constant.
misconceptions.misconception: Pressure is proportional to volume, so squashing the gas into a smaller volume lowers the pressure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Direct proportion is the default relationship students assume between any two quantities.
misconceptions.correction: p V = constant is an inverse relationship. Halving the volume doubles the pressure: 200 kPa in 0.50 m³ becomes 500 kPa in 0.20 m³.

misconceptions.question: Does the pressure of a fixed mass of gas change when its volume is changed at constant temperature?
misconceptions.correct: Yes - the pressure changes so that the product p V stays the same.
misconceptions.misconception: Pressure is a property of the gas, so it stays the same whatever the container does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Pressure is confused with a fixed material property such as density at a given temperature.
misconceptions.correction: Compressing the gas makes the particles hit the walls more often, raising the pressure. p V = constant predicts 500 kPa when 0.50 m³ at 200 kPa is squeezed to 0.20 m³.

mcqs.stem: A question gives a mass of 250 g and a time of 2.0 minutes. Which pair of values should be substituted so that the working is in standard SI units?

options.rationale: 250 g = 0.25 kg and 2.0 minutes = 120 s, the SI units of mass and time.
The time is converted but the number of grams is treated as if it were already kilograms.
The mass is converted but the minutes are substituted as though they were seconds.
The values are copied straight from the question with no conversion at all.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the equations in the first list of Appendix A?

options.text: They are printed on the equation sheet for both tiers
options.rationale: Students who have seen the sheet in class assume every equation appears on it.

options.text: They must be recognised but never rearranged or used
options.rationale: Recall is reduced to spotting the equation rather than using it.

options.text: They must be recalled from memory and then applied
options.rationale: The first list is the recall list; the equation sheet carries only the second list.

options.text: They are needed for Higher Tier papers only, not both
options.rationale: The HT label is assumed to apply to the whole list rather than to single equations.

mcqs.stem: A rock has a mass of 12 kg. Gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the weight of the rock?

options.rationale: The mass number is quoted as the weight because the two are treated as the same quantity.
The calculation is right but the answer is given in the unit of mass.
The mass has been divided by g instead of multiplied by it.
W = m g = 12 × 9.8 = 117.6 N, which is 118 N to three significant figures.

mcqs.stem: A 60 kg astronaut travels to the Moon, where g is about 1.6 N/kg. Which row is correct?

options.text: The mass falls to 10 kg and the weight falls to 96 N
options.rationale: Mass and weight are treated as the same quantity, so both are scaled down.

options.text: The mass stays 60 kg and the weight stays at 588 N
options.rationale: Weight is imagined as a fixed property belonging to the astronaut.

options.text: The mass stays 60 kg and the weight falls to 96 N
options.rationale: Mass is unchanged by location; W = 60 × 1.6 = 96 N on the Moon.

options.text: The mass falls to 10 kg and the weight stays 588 N
options.rationale: The scaling is applied to the wrong quantity of the two.

mcqs.stem: A shopper holds a bag with a steady vertical upward force of 40 N and walks 5.0 m along level ground. How much work is done by that upward force?

options.rationale: Force is multiplied by the distance walked, ignoring the direction of the force.
There is no distance moved along the line of action of the vertical force, so no work is done by it.
The force has been divided by the distance instead of multiplied.
The two numbers are added when the student cannot decide on the operation.

mcqs.stem: A spring of unstretched length 12 cm is stretched to 20 cm by a force of 4.0 N. What is the spring constant?

options.rationale: The stretched length of 0.20 m is used in place of the extension.
The extension is left in centimetres, giving 4.0/8.0.
The force is multiplied by the extension instead of divided by it.

mcqs.stem: A force of 30 N is applied at the end of a spanner of length 0.25 m. The distance from the pivot normal to the direction of the force is 0.20 m. What is the moment?

options.rationale: The length of the spanner is used instead of the perpendicular distance.
The force is divided by the distance rather than multiplied by it.
M = F d uses the distance normal to the force: 30 × 0.20 = 6.0 N m.
The force is repeated as the answer and given the unit of the data.

mcqs.stem: A crate presses on the floor with a force of 600 N normal to the surface, over a contact area of 0.30 m². What is the pressure?

options.rationale: The force is multiplied by the area instead of divided by it.
The arithmetic is right but the answer is labelled with the unit of force.
The area has been divided by the force.

mcqs.stem: A cyclist travels at a steady speed of 6.0 m/s for 4.0 minutes. What distance is travelled?

options.rationale: The time is substituted as 4.0 s instead of 240 s.
The time has been divided by the speed.
The speed has been divided by the time.

mcqs.stem: A car speeds up from 8.0 m/s to 20 m/s in 4.0 s. What is its acceleration?

options.rationale: The final velocity is divided by the time, ignoring the change.
The two velocities are added instead of subtracted before dividing.
The time has been divided by the change in velocity.

mcqs.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg has a driving force of 4000 N and resistive forces totalling 1000 N. What is its acceleration?

options.rationale: Resultant force = 4000 − 1000 = 3000 N, so a = F/m = 3000/1200 = 2.5 m/s².
Only the driving force is used, so the resistive forces are ignored.
The two forces are added rather than subtracted to find the resultant.
The resistive force alone is divided by the mass.

mcqs.stem: A ball of mass 0.45 kg moves at 12 m/s. What is its momentum?

options.rationale: The velocity is squared, as it would be for kinetic energy.
The arithmetic is right but momentum is labelled as a force.
The mass has been divided by the velocity.

mcqs.stem: A runner of mass 60 kg moves at 4.0 m/s. What is the runner's kinetic energy?

options.rationale: The speed is not squared, giving 0.5 × 60 × 4.0.
The speed is squared but the factor of 0.5 is omitted.
Both the square and the half are dropped, leaving 60 × 4.0.

mcqs.stem: The speed of a car doubles while its mass stays the same. What happens to its kinetic energy?

options.text: It doubles, in step with the speed
options.rationale: The relationship is assumed to be directly proportional.

options.text: It becomes four times as large
options.rationale: E_k depends on v², and doubling v multiplies v² by four.

options.text: It becomes eight times as large
options.rationale: The doubling is applied on top of the squaring as well.

options.text: It stays the same, as mass is fixed
options.rationale: Kinetic energy is treated as a property of the mass alone.

mcqs.stem: A box of mass 2.0 kg is pushed 5.0 m along a ramp and rises 1.5 m vertically. Gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the gain in gravitational potential energy?

options.rationale: The 5.0 m measured along the ramp is used instead of the vertical height.
The gravitational field strength is left out of the product.
E_p = m g h = 2.0 × 9.8 × 1.5 = 29.4 J, using the vertical height.
Mass, ramp length and height are multiplied together and g is omitted.

mcqs.stem: A kettle transfers 360 000 J of energy in 180 s. What is its power?

options.rationale: The energy transferred is quoted as the power, as if they were the same.
The time is quoted as the answer without any calculation.
The time has been divided by the energy transferred.

mcqs.stem: A crane does 24 000 J of work in 30 s. What is its power output?

options.rationale: The work done is multiplied by the time instead of divided by it.
The work done is relabelled as the power.
The time has been divided by the work done.

mcqs.stem: An electric motor transfers 250 J usefully from a total input of 1000 J. What is its efficiency?

options.rationale: The fraction is inverted so that the larger number is on top.
efficiency = useful output / total input = 250/1000 = 0.25.
The 750 J wasted is used in place of the useful output.
The wasted energy is quoted as though efficiency were an amount of energy.

mcqs.stem: A lamp has a useful power output of 6.0 W and a total power input of 40 W. What is its efficiency as a percentage?

options.rationale: efficiency = 6.0/40 = 0.15, which is 15%.
The powers are divided the wrong way round, giving an impossible efficiency.
The 34 W wasted is compared with the input instead of the useful output.
The difference between the two powers is quoted as a percentage.

mcqs.stem: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 0.60 m. What is its speed?

options.rationale: The frequency is divided by the wavelength instead of multiplied.
The arithmetic is right but the answer takes the unit of the frequency.
The wavelength has been divided by the frequency.

mcqs.stem: A current of 0.50 A flows through a lamp for 4.0 minutes. How much charge flows?

options.rationale: The time is substituted as 4.0 s rather than 240 s.
The current value is quoted as the charge, treating them as one quantity.
The time has been divided by the current.
Q = I t = 0.50 × 240 = 120 C, with the time converted to seconds.

mcqs.stem: A resistor of resistance 12 Ω carries a current of 0.25 A. What is the potential difference across it?

options.rationale: The resistance is divided by the current instead of multiplied.
The current is divided by the resistance.
The arithmetic is right but the answer is labelled with the unit of current.

mcqs.stem: A lamp works at a potential difference of 230 V and draws a current of 0.26 A. What is its power?

options.rationale: The potential difference is divided by the current.
The power is correct but is given the unit of energy.
P = V I = 230 × 0.26 = 59.8 W, which is 60 W to two significant figures.
The potential difference is quoted as the power.

mcqs.stem: A current of 3.0 A passes through a resistor of resistance 20 Ω. What is the power dissipated?

options.rationale: The resistance is squared instead of the current.
The current and resistance are simply multiplied, with no squaring.
The resistance is divided by the current.

mcqs.stem: A 2000 W heater is switched on for 5.0 minutes. How much energy is transferred?

options.rationale: The time is substituted as 5.0 s rather than 300 s.
The power is divided by the time in minutes.
The power rating is quoted as the energy transferred.
E = P t = 2000 × 300 = 600 000 J, with the time converted to seconds.

mcqs.stem: A charge of 15 C flows through a component with a potential difference of 12 V across it. How much energy is transferred?

options.rationale: The charge is divided by the potential difference.
The value is right but the answer takes the unit of charge.
The potential difference is divided by the charge.

mcqs.stem: A metal block has a mass of 5.4 kg and a volume of 0.0020 m³. What is its density?

options.rationale: The volume is divided by the mass.
The mass is multiplied by the volume instead of divided by it.
The number is right but the unit of mass is used for a density.

mcqs.stem: Which of these equations is printed on the Physics equation sheet rather than having to be recalled?

options.text: gravitational potential energy = mass × gravitational field strength × height
options.rationale: Its length makes students assume it must be provided, but it is a recall equation.

options.text: efficiency = useful output energy transfer / total input energy transfer
options.rationale: Students who believe every equation is supplied pick any long equation here.

options.text: work done = force × distance along the line of action of the force
options.rationale: The bracketed condition makes it look like sheet wording, but it must be recalled.

options.text: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
options.rationale: This is equation 5 of the second Appendix A list, so it is provided on the sheet.

mcqs.stem: A tank holds water of density 1000 kg/m³ to a depth of 3.0 m. Gravitational field strength is 9.8 N/kg. What is the pressure due to the column of water at the bottom?

options.rationale: The gravitational field strength is left out of the product.
The depth is omitted, as though pressure did not depend on it.
A place-value slip of ten, typical when g is handled carelessly.

mcqs.stem: A car travelling at 5.0 m/s accelerates at 2.0 m/s² over a distance of 12 m. What is its final velocity?

options.rationale: The value of v² is quoted without taking the square root.
The initial velocity term is dropped, leaving v² = 2 a s = 48.
The u² term is subtracted rather than added when rearranging.

mcqs.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 15 m/s is brought to rest in 0.20 s in a crash. What is the average force on the car?

options.rationale: The change in momentum is multiplied by the time instead of divided by it.
The change in momentum is quoted as the force, with no division by time.
The mass is left out, giving only ∆v/∆t.

mcqs.stem: A spring with a spring constant of 200 N/m is extended by 0.30 m. How much elastic potential energy is stored?

options.rationale: F = k e is used, which gives the force of 60 N and not an energy.
The extension is not squared, giving 0.5 × 200 × 0.30.
The extension is squared but the factor of 0.5 is omitted.

mcqs.stem: 2.0 kg of water with a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. What is the change in thermal energy?

options.rationale: The final temperature of 70 °C is used instead of the 50 °C change.
The temperature change is left out of the product altogether.
The starting temperature of 20 °C is substituted for the change.

mcqs.stem: A wave has a frequency of 250 Hz. What is its period?

options.rationale: period = 1/frequency = 1/250 = 0.0040 s.
The frequency value is quoted as the period.
The value is right but the answer takes the unit of frequency.
The frequency is treated as 0.25 of something rather than 250 Hz.

mcqs.stem: An object 4.0 mm tall produces an image 26 mm tall. What is the magnification?

options.rationale: The object height is divided by the image height.
The ratio is right but a unit is attached to it.
magnification = image height / object height = 26/4.0 = 6.5.
The heights are subtracted rather than divided.

mcqs.stem: A conductor of length 0.25 m carries a current of 3.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.40 T. What is the force on the conductor?

options.rationale: The length of the conductor is left out of the product.
The product B I is divided by the length instead of multiplied.
The flux density is left out and current times length is used.

mcqs.stem: 0.50 kg of ice at 0 °C melts completely. The specific latent heat of fusion of water is 340 000 J/kg. How much thermal energy is needed?

options.rationale: The specific latent heat is quoted as though it were the total energy.
The specific latent heat is divided by the mass instead of multiplied.
The value is right but an energy is given the unit of power.

mcqs.stem: A transformer has 200 turns on the primary coil and 1000 turns on the secondary coil. The potential difference across the primary is 230 V. What is the potential difference across the secondary?

options.rationale: The turns ratio is applied upside down, so the pd is stepped down.
The transformer is assumed to leave the potential difference unchanged.
The ratio is inverted and a factor of ten is lost as well.

mcqs.stem: A transformer is 100% efficient. Its primary coil takes 2.0 A at 230 V and the potential difference across the secondary is 1150 V. What is the current in the secondary coil?

options.rationale: The equation is used upside down, so the current is stepped up as well as the pd.
The current is assumed to be the same in both coils.
The primary power is quoted as though it were the secondary current.

mcqs.stem: A fixed mass of gas at a pressure of 200 kPa occupies 0.50 m³. It is compressed at constant temperature to 0.20 m³. What is the new pressure?

options.rationale: Pressure is assumed to fall in proportion with the volume.
p V = constant, so p = 200 × 0.50/0.20 = 500 kPa.
The pressure is treated as a fixed property of the gas.
The volumes are multiplied rather than used as a ratio.
